author: @Timo_NFL
title_or_hook: From Pressure to Sack: a frame-level study of pressure, threat, and QB response (main post; also feed row 3)
summary: A frame-level (tracking) study by Timo Riske at SumerSports: for every play, a time series of P(pressure), P(a given rusher generates the pressure), and P(sack). Its key construction defines a 'threat' before pressure arrives, splitting QB response into sack danger at pressure arrival (a rusher/context property), sack avoidance beyond that expectation (a QB property), and response choice (quick release, hold and maneuver, or leave the pocket). Findings as stated: for rushers, whatever stability exists in sacks-per-pressure comes from danger at arrival; for QBs, both danger at arrival and avoidance beyond it are stable traits; releasing quickly after a threat is the most efficient response on average, but EPA on quick releases before incoming pressure is notably unstable, while what happens after the QB holds the ball (pocket maneuvering, escaping) is stable. The author's own caveat: the QB sample has an era gap (Brady/Brees/Rivers/Roethlisberger era vs Mahomes-and-later), so cross-era QB comparisons on this metric carry a structural hole. Article takeaways are CITED from the browser's read of the article page and thread, not from reproduced data; the frame-level model is SumerSports' proprietary tracking model.

author: @The_Coach_A
title_or_hook: Bowles' Hot blitz plan vs Chicago's 11 personnel: two INTs on throwaways; Traditional - Fire Zone - Hot taught through his Cover 3 base
summary: Three scheme mechanisms in the author's own words. (a) Hot blitzing: Flores made it a main element in 2023; Bowles now carries it. Against Chicago his plan attacked the Bears' 11 personnel, kept Caleb Williams from getting comfortable, and produced two interceptions on throwaways. Bowles teaches the coverage behind it through his Cover 3 base: Traditional, Fire Zone, and Hot are three ways to teach the same family. (b) The Chiefs' Fire Zone path: Spagnuolo uses the traditional Fire Zone path (no cross) moved one gap over, to the weak side as well, substituting his CB for the Safety as the added rusher; the DE becomes the contain rush. (c) The Cross path: a pressure that attacks gun runs and creates negative plays; the Vikings example vs the Packers' pin-pull: the alignment triggers the C and LG to pull, leaving nobody to block back on the Mike through the A-gap. Single-source film reads, CITED; the two-INT claim is the author's game-plan account, not a reproduced count; the linked MatchQuarters breakdown was not opened this run.

title_or_hook: 'Cache or Denoise Less?' - flow-matching world model paper (arXiv:2611.19709) with code: 2 uncached steps beat an 8-step cache (feed row 19)
summary: A negative-result systems paper with a clean method (CoRL 2026 EEAI Workshop; authors Abhinav Gupta and Nissan Pow, per the repo README as read by the browser). Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated denoising steps; cross-cycle caches (C3ache) reuse computation across replanning calls. The paper asks whether caching beats simply taking fewer steps, in Fast-WAM (a 6B-parameter world action model) on LIBERO-Goal. Results from the repo README table (browser-read this run): uncached 10 steps = 202 ms/call, 95.0% success; uncached 2 steps = 92-94 ms, 95.0-96.0% success (non-inferior within 2 points on all 500 initial states, one checkpoint, one noise seed); uncached 1 step = 81 ms but success drops to 88-93%; C3ache with 8 cached steps = 100 ms and success collapses to 63.0% under the s=1 time schedule (94.0% under s=5); a composed cache saves at most about 11-14%. The structural argument: a cache keeping two fresh steps cannot beat two uncached steps, because every call still pays the encoding and expert costs. Numbers are VERIFIED at the repo README level; the paper PDF itself was not read this run.
